title: Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing
text: 1 Introduction
crumbs: 1  Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing

title: Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing
text:
1.1 Project Background
High-performance computing (HPC) is an important part of Australia’s research infrastructure, supporting computationally intensive research across a wide range of scientific fields.
Australia has two national Tier-1 HPC facilities accessible to researchers: the National Computational Infrastructure (NCI) and the Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre. Several Tier-2 HPC facilities also operate across Australian research institutions.
As research becomes increasingly data- and compute-intensive, understanding future demand for HPC resources is important for planning Australia’s national research infrastructure.
crumbs: 1  Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing

title: Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing
text:
1.2 Project Purpose
The purpose of this project is to develop a robust forecast of Australian research demand for high-performance computing to 2030.
The forecast is intended to support national policy discussions around public compute investment and future research infrastructure planning.
The project combines data engineering, descriptive analysis and forecasting using historical Australian HPC data and other indicators that may help explain changes in research compute demand.
crumbs: 1  Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing

title: Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing
text:
1.3 The Forecasting Problem
One of the main challenges is that observed HPC allocation does not necessarily represent actual research demand.
National allocation schemes operate under limited available capacity. As a result, allocated compute represents the amount of resource awarded rather than necessarily the amount researchers required.
Requested compute provides additional information about demand, but may also underestimate actual need if researchers limit their requests based on expected availability or if potential users do not apply.
The project therefore distinguishes between:

requested compute,
allocated compute,
the observed gap between requested and allocated compute, and
underlying or latent demand.
crumbs: 1  Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing

title: Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing
text:
1.4 Project Objectives
The project aims to:

build a documented longitudinal dataset of Australian HPC activity,
improve comparability of compute measures across years, facilities and hardware generations,
distinguish CPU and GPU compute where possible,
examine historical demand, allocation and oversubscription,
analyse changes in Field of Research composition,
investigate potential structural drivers of HPC demand,
develop and compare suitable forecasting models,
forecast HPC demand to 2030 under different scenarios, and
estimate potential future gaps between demand and available capacity.
crumbs: 1  Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing

title: Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing
text:
1.5 Analysis Framework
The analysis follows ten main steps:

Data collection
Potential variable definition
Data integration
Data standardisation
Data conversion
Initial analysis and data manipulation
Model development and benchmarking
Model evaluation
Model selection
Scenario forecasting and capacity-gap analysis
crumbs: 1  Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing

title: 2  Data Collection
text:
2.1 Purpose
The first step of the project was to collect historical data on Australian HPC demand and allocation, together with other variables that may help explain changes in research compute demand over time.
The data collection focused on building a longitudinal dataset that could support both descriptive analysis and forecasting.

title: 2  Data Collection
text:
2.2 Data Sources
Data was collected from several sources, including:

National Computational Merit Allocation Scheme (NCMAS) outcomes and supporting documentation,
National Computational Infrastructure (NCI) annual reports and publications,
Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre annual reports and publications,
Australian Research Council (ARC) funding data,
National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) funding data,
Medical Research Future Fund (MRFF) data,
research workforce and research activity data, and
Field of Research (FoR) information.

International HPC data will also be considered where suitable data is available, including information from EuroHPC, NSF ACCESS and ARCHER2.

title: 2  Data Collection
text:
2.3 HPC Demand and Allocation Data
The main HPC dataset currently covers the period from 2013/14 to 2025/26.
The collected information includes, where available:

requested compute,
allocated compute,
facility,
HPC system,
resource type,
original compute unit,
Field of Research,
institution,
source, and
reporting period.

The level of detail varies across years because historical reporting practices and available public information are not consistent throughout the full period.

title: 2  Data Collection
text:
2.4 Field of Research Data
Field of Research information was collected to examine how the composition of HPC use has changed over time.
Where possible, historical FoR classifications are mapped to a consistent classification to support comparison across years.
The available FoR data primarily describes the composition of allocated compute. It should therefore not automatically be interpreted as the composition of underlying research demand.

title: 2  Data Collection
text:
2.5 Potential Demand Drivers
Additional datasets are being collected to investigate structural drivers of HPC demand.
These include research funding, workforce, research activity and other indicators that may be associated with changes in research compute requirements.
The suitability of these variables for forecasting will be assessed later based on their historical coverage, consistency and relationship with HPC demand.

title: 2  Data Collection
text:
2.6 Data Provenance
The original source, reporting period, reported unit and relevant notes are retained wherever possible.
This allows subsequent transformations and assumptions to be traced back to the original data source and helps identify observations that may not be directly comparable across years.

title: 2  Data Collection
text:
2.7 Data Collection Limitations
The main limitations identified during data collection include:

limited consistent data before 2013,
differences in reporting formats across years,
inconsistent availability of requested and allocated compute,
incomplete separation of CPU and GPU resources in some historical data,
changes in HPC systems and accounting methods, and
differences in FoR classifications over time.

These issues are addressed in the subsequent data integration, standardisation and conversion stages.

title: 3  Potential Variable Definition
text:
3.1 Purpose
The second step is to define the variables that may be used in the descriptive analysis and forecasting models.
The variables are divided into three main groups:
The final variables used in the forecasting models will depend on data availability, consistency and the results of the exploratory analysis.

title: 3  Potential Variable Definition
text:
target variables representing HPC demand,
allocation and capacity variables, and
potential structural drivers of HPC demand.

title: 3  Potential Variable Definition
text:
3.2 HPC Demand
The main outcome of interest is Australian research demand for HPC resources.
However, demand is not directly observed in a single consistent measure. The project therefore distinguishes between several concepts.

3.2.1 Requested Compute
Requested compute represents the amount of HPC resource requested through allocation schemes where this information is available.
This provides an observable indicator of demand, but it may not represent the full level of research need if researchers limit their requests based on expected availability or if potential users do not apply.
Where possible, requested compute will be separated into:

requested CPU core-hours; and
requested GPU-hours.



3.2.2 Allocated Compute
Allocated compute represents the amount of HPC resource awarded to researchers.
Allocation is treated separately from demand because it is constrained by the amount of compute available and by the allocation process.
Where possible, allocated compute will be separated into:

allocated CPU core-hours; and
allocated GPU-hours.



3.2.3 Latent Demand
Latent demand refers to the underlying level of HPC resources that Australian researchers may require, including demand that is not fully observed through allocation or request data.
Latent demand is not directly observed and will therefore need to be estimated using available demand indicators and structural drivers.

title: 3  Potential Variable Definition
text:
3.3 Demand and Allocation Indicators
Several indicators can be derived from the historical data.
The observed request-allocation gap is defined as:
\[
\text{Request-Allocation Gap}_t =
\text{Requested Compute}_t -
\text{Allocated Compute}_t
\]
The fulfilment rate is defined as:
\[
\text{Fulfilment Rate}_t =
\frac{\text{Allocated Compute}_t}
{\text{Requested Compute}_t}
\]
These measures can help describe the relationship between observed requests and available allocation over time.
They should not automatically be interpreted as the full level of unmet demand because requested compute itself may be constrained.

title: 3  Potential Variable Definition
text:
3.4 Field of Research
Field of Research (FoR) is used to examine differences in the composition of HPC activity across research disciplines.
Potential FoR variables include:

FoR classification,
share of annual allocation by FoR,
allocated compute by FoR, and
changes in FoR composition over time.

The currently available FoR information primarily represents allocation rather than directly observed requested demand. Any use of allocation composition as a proxy for demand composition will therefore be documented as an assumption.

title: 3  Potential Variable Definition
text:
3.5 Potential Structural Drivers
The project will investigate variables that may help explain changes in HPC demand over time.
Potential drivers include:

3.5.1 Research Funding

Australian Research Council (ARC) funding,
National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) funding,
Medical Research Future Fund (MRFF) funding, and
broader research and development expenditure where suitable data is available.



3.5.2 Research Workforce and Activity

research workforce size,
number of researchers,
PhD completions,
number of research projects, and
grant activity in compute-intensive research fields.



3.5.3 Compute Intensity
Potential indicators of changing compute intensity include:

compute use per project,
compute use by Field of Research,
changes in CPU and GPU use, and
changes associated with increasingly compute-intensive research.



3.5.4 HPC Infrastructure
Infrastructure variables may include:

available HPC systems,
system commissioning and retirement,
available CPU and GPU resources, and
changes in national compute capacity.

These variables are important for distinguishing changes in demand from changes caused by additional supply.

title: 3  Potential Variable Definition
text:
3.6 International Benchmarking Variables
Where suitable data is available, international HPC systems may be used as external benchmarks.
Potential indicators include:

compute per researcher,
compute per research dollar,
allocation and utilisation, and
changes in CPU and GPU use.

Potential international comparators include EuroHPC, NSF ACCESS and ARCHER2.

title: 3  Potential Variable Definition
text:
3.7 Variable Selection for Modelling
Not all potential variables will necessarily be included in the final forecasting model.
Variable selection will consider:

theoretical relevance to HPC demand,
historical data coverage,
consistency of measurement,
availability through the forecast horizon,
relationship with observed HPC demand, and
the limited number of annual observations available for modelling.

The final model will prioritise a small number of interpretable variables rather than including a large number of predictors in a short annual time series.

title: 4  Data Integration
text:
4.1 Purpose
The purpose of this step is to integrate the different data sources collected for the project into a consistent structure for analysis.
The datasets were collected from different sources and contain different time periods, levels of detail, and reporting formats. Integration is therefore required before the variables can be compared and used for modelling.

title: 4  Data Integration
text:
4.2 Main Datasets
The main datasets used in the integration process are:

HPC demand and allocation data
NCMAS project and allocation data
Field of Research data
Research funding data
Research workforce and activity data
HPC system and capacity information

title: 4  Data Integration
text:
4.3 Time Period
The main HPC dataset covers the period from 2013/14 to 2025/26.
Other datasets may have different reporting periods. Where possible, these are aligned with the corresponding HPC allocation year while retaining the original reporting period for reference.

title: 4  Data Integration
text:
4.4 Integration Structure
The datasets are integrated primarily using:

year or reporting period
Field of Research
institution, where available
facility and HPC system
resource type

The level of integration depends on the detail available in each source.

title: 4  Data Integration
text:
4.5 Integration Considerations
Several issues need to be considered when integrating the datasets:

reporting periods are not always consistent across sources
Field of Research classifications have changed over time
institution names may be reported differently
CPU and GPU resources are reported using different units
some historical demand values are directly reported while others are estimated or derived
the level of detail available varies across years

These differences are retained and documented rather than assuming that all observations are directly comparable.

title: 4  Data Integration
text:
4.6 Output
The output of this step is an integrated dataset that retains the original source information while providing a common structure for subsequent data standardisation and conversion.

title: 5  Data Standardisation
text:
5.1 Purpose
The purpose of this step is to standardise variables that are reported differently across years and data sources.
The historical HPC data were collected from multiple reports and datasets. Differences in terminology, classification, units, and reporting structure need to be addressed before the data can be compared over time.

title: 5  Data Standardisation
text:
5.2 Reporting Period
Reporting periods are standardised into a consistent annual format, while the original reporting period is retained for reference.
The main analysis currently covers 2013/14 to 2025/26.

title: 5  Data Standardisation
text:
5.3 Institution Names
Institution names may vary across datasets and years due to abbreviations, naming conventions, or organisational changes.
Where possible, institution names are mapped to a consistent name while retaining the originally reported value.

title: 5  Data Standardisation
text:
5.4 Field of Research Classification
Field of Research classifications are not fully consistent across the historical period.
Earlier observations may use the 2008 Australian and New Zealand Standard Research Classification (ANZSRC), while more recent observations may use the 2020 classification.
Where possible, research fields are mapped to a common classification for longitudinal analysis. The original classification is retained to avoid losing information from the source data.

title: 5  Data Standardisation
text:
5.5 HPC Facilities and Systems
Facility and system names are standardised so that allocations can be associated with the relevant HPC infrastructure.
This is particularly important because different systems may use different service unit accounting methods.

title: 5  Data Standardisation
text:
5.6 Resource Type
Compute resources are classified into resource types where sufficient information is available.
The main distinction is between:

CPU resources
GPU resources
mixed or unspecified resources

CPU and GPU resources are kept separate because they represent different types of computing resources and cannot be directly combined as physical compute hours.

title: 5  Data Standardisation
text:
5.7 Units
The original reported unit is retained for each observation.
Historical sources may report compute using units such as:

service units (SU)
kilo service units (kSU)
CPU core-hours
GPU hours
other reported compute-hour measures

Unit labels are standardised at this stage, but conversion between units is handled separately in the data conversion step.

title: 5  Data Standardisation
text:
5.8 Data Quality and Comparability
Additional indicators are used where necessary to identify differences in data quality and comparability.
These may include whether a value is:

directly reported
derived from another reported value
estimated or used as a proxy
comparable across years
affected by changes in systems or reporting methods

These indicators allow later analysis to distinguish between directly observed values and values that require additional assumptions.

title: 5  Data Standardisation
text:
5.9 Output
The output of this step is a standardised dataset that retains the original reported information while providing consistent classifications for subsequent conversion and analysis.

title: 6  Data Conversion
text:
6.1 Purpose
The purpose of this step is to convert the reported HPC resource values into units that are more comparable across years and systems.
The historical data are reported using different units, including service units (SU), kilo service units (kSU), CPU core-hours and GPU hours. Service unit accounting can also differ between HPC systems and resource types. Therefore, a single conversion factor cannot be applied across the full historical dataset.

title: 6  Data Conversion
text:
6.2 Conversion Approach
The original reported value and unit are retained in the dataset.
Where sufficient information is available, reported service units are converted using conversion factors specific to the relevant facility, system and resource type.
The general conversion from kSU to SU is:
\[
\text{SU} = \text{kSU} \times 1000
\]
Conversion from SU to physical compute hours depends on the accounting method used by the relevant HPC system.

title: 6  Data Conversion
text:
6.3 CPU Resources
CPU resources are converted to CPU core-hours where a documented service-unit conversion is available.
For example, if a system charges two service units per CPU core-hour:
\[
\text{CPU Core-Hours}
=
\frac{\text{kSU} \times 1000}{2}
\]
The applicable conversion factor is determined separately for each system and reporting period.

title: 6  Data Conversion
6  Data Conversion
text:
6.5 Historical Conversion
Conversion of historical observations requires additional care because HPC systems and service-unit accounting methods have changed over time.
For each observation, the conversion process considers:

facility
HPC system
reporting period
resource type
original unit
documented service-unit accounting method

Where a reliable conversion factor cannot be identified, the original reported value is retained rather than applying an unsupported conversion.

title: 6  Data Conversion
text:
6.6 Conversion Documentation
The converted dataset retains information about how each value was produced.
Where possible, this includes:

original reported value
original reported unit
converted value
converted unit
conversion formula or factor
conversion source
conversion confidence
comparability status
relevant notes

This allows converted values to be traced back to their original source and assumptions.

title: 6  Data Conversion
text:
6.7 CPU and GPU Separation
CPU core-hours and GPU hours are maintained as separate measures throughout the analysis.
This avoids treating different computational resources as directly equivalent and allows changes in the composition of HPC demand, including increasing GPU demand, to be analysed separately.

title: 6  Data Conversion
text:
6.8 Current Limitations
Conversion factors have not yet been confirmed for every historical system and year.
In particular, historical service-unit accounting and changes associated with system transitions require further validation. These assumptions will be reviewed using available documentation and feedback from NCI and Pawsey before the final converted dataset is used for modelling.

title: 6  Data Conversion
text:
6.9 Output
The output of this step will be a conversion table and analysis dataset containing the original reported values together with comparable CPU or GPU measures where supported by sufficient evidence.

title: 7  Initial Analysis and Data Manipulation
text:
7.1 Purpose
The purpose of this step is to explore the prepared datasets, identify historical patterns, assess data quality and comparability, and prepare the variables required for modelling.
This analysis is also used to identify potential relationships between HPC demand and the structural drivers considered in the project.
crumbs: 7  Initial Analysis and Data Manipulation

title: 7  Initial Analysis and Data Manipulation
text:
7.2 Historical Demand and Allocation
Historical requested and allocated compute are examined over time to understand how the use of national HPC resources has changed.
The analysis considers:

changes in requested compute
changes in allocated compute
the gap between requested and allocated resources
fulfilment rates
periods of unusually high or low growth

Requested and allocated compute are interpreted separately because allocation is constrained by available capacity and does not necessarily represent total research demand.
crumbs: 7  Initial Analysis and Data Manipulation

title: 7  Initial Analysis and Data Manipulation
text:
7.3 CPU and GPU Resources
Where sufficient information is available, CPU and GPU resources are analysed separately.
This allows the analysis to examine:

historical CPU demand and allocation
historical GPU demand and allocation
changes in the composition of national HPC usage
the increasing role of GPU-based computing

CPU core-hours and GPU hours are not combined into a single physical compute measure.
crumbs: 7  Initial Analysis and Data Manipulation

title: 7  Initial Analysis and Data Manipulation
text:
7.4 Field of Research
The distribution of HPC resources across Fields of Research is examined to identify which research areas account for the largest shares of national compute allocation and how this composition has changed over time.
Where FoR data represent allocation rather than requested compute, this distinction is retained when interpreting the results.
crumbs: 7  Initial Analysis and Data Manipulation

title: 7  Initial Analysis and Data Manipulation
text:
7.5 Institutional Distribution
Where institution-level data are available, allocations are examined across universities and research organisations.
This provides an indication of how national HPC resources are distributed across institutions and whether the distribution has changed over time.
crumbs: 7  Initial Analysis and Data Manipulation

title: 7  Initial Analysis and Data Manipulation
text:
7.6 Potential Demand Drivers
Potential structural drivers are explored alongside the HPC data.
These may include:

research funding
research workforce
research activity
grant funding in compute-intensive fields
changes in compute intensity
changes in HPC infrastructure

The purpose of this analysis is to identify variables that may be useful for the modelling stage rather than assuming that every available variable should be included.
crumbs: 7  Initial Analysis and Data Manipulation

title: 7  Initial Analysis and Data Manipulation
text:
7.7 Data Manipulation for Modelling
Additional variables required for analysis and modelling are created where appropriate.
These may include:

annual growth rates
request-allocation gaps
fulfilment rates
lagged funding variables
FoR shares
indicators for major system changes
CPU and GPU measures

Any derived variables and assumptions are documented so that they can be reproduced.
crumbs: 7  Initial Analysis and Data Manipulation

title: 7  Initial Analysis and Data Manipulation
text:
7.8 Exploratory Analysis
Visual and statistical analysis is used to examine trends, relationships and potential structural changes in the data.
This includes time-series plots, comparisons between requested and allocated compute, FoR composition, and relationships between HPC demand and potential structural drivers.
Particular attention is given to major changes in national HPC infrastructure because increases in observed allocation may reflect changes in available capacity rather than equivalent increases in underlying demand.
crumbs: 7  Initial Analysis and Data Manipulation

title: 7  Initial Analysis and Data Manipulation
text:
7.9 Data Readiness for Modelling
Before moving to model development, the prepared data are assessed for:

sufficient historical coverage
consistency of units
CPU and GPU separation
availability of requested and allocated values
direct versus derived or proxy observations
changes in HPC systems
changes in FoR classifications
missing values
potential structural breaks

Variables that are not sufficiently comparable or supported by the available data are either excluded from modelling or treated separately.
crumbs: 7  Initial Analysis and Data Manipulation

title: 7  Initial Analysis and Data Manipulation
text:
7.10 Output
The output of this step is a modelling-ready dataset together with an initial understanding of historical HPC demand, allocation, research composition and potential demand drivers.
These findings provide the basis for model development and benchmarking in the next step.
crumbs: 7  Initial Analysis and Data Manipulation

title: 8  Model Development and Benchmarking
text:
8.1 Purpose
The purpose of this step is to develop forecasting models for Australian research HPC demand and compare their performance.
The modelling approach includes simple benchmark models as well as models that incorporate potential structural drivers of HPC demand.
Because the historical dataset is relatively short and includes changes in HPC systems, reporting methods and resource types, the models are kept relatively simple and interpretable.

title: 8  Model Development and Benchmarking
text:
8.2 Forecast Target
The primary forecasting target is Australian research demand for national HPC resources.
Where the available data support it, CPU and GPU demand are modelled separately because they represent different types of computational resources and have different historical growth patterns.
Allocated compute is treated separately from demand because allocation is constrained by available national HPC capacity.

title: 8  Model Development and Benchmarking
text:
8.3 Benchmark Models
Simple forecasting models are used to provide a baseline against which more complex models can be compared.
The benchmark models considered include:

naïve
drift
linear trend
exponential smoothing (ETS)
ARIMA

These models provide different representations of the historical trend without requiring external explanatory variables.

title: 8  Model Development and Benchmarking
text:
8.4 Structural Demand Model
In addition to the benchmark models, a structural modelling approach is considered to explain HPC demand using potential demand drivers.
Potential drivers identified in the earlier stages include:

research funding
research workforce
research activity
funding in compute-intensive research fields
compute intensity
changes in CPU and GPU use

A general form of the structural model is:
\[
D_t =
\beta_0 +
\beta_1 X_{1,t} +
\beta_2 X_{2,t} +
\cdots +
\beta_k X_{k,t} +
\varepsilon_t
\]
where \(D_t\) represents HPC demand and \(X_{1,t}, \ldots, X_{k,t}\) represent selected demand drivers.

title: 8  Model Development and Benchmarking
text:
8.5 Leading Indicators
Some structural variables may influence HPC demand with a delay.
For example, research funding may be considered as a leading indicator because funded research projects may require HPC resources after funding has been awarded.
Where supported by the data, lagged variables are therefore considered:
\[
D_t =
\beta_0 +
\beta_1 Funding_{t-1} +
\beta_2 Workforce_t +
\beta_3 ComputeIntensity_t +
\varepsilon_t
\]
The appropriate lag structure is determined using the available data and the expected relationship between each driver and HPC demand.

title: 8  Model Development and Benchmarking
text:
8.6 Variable Selection
The number of predictors included in the structural model is kept small because the historical annual dataset contains a limited number of observations.
Variables are considered based on:

theoretical relationship with HPC demand
historical data availability
consistency across years
exploratory relationships with demand
availability of future values or assumptions to 2030
interpretability for policy analysis

Variables are not included solely because they improve in-sample model fit.

title: 8  Model Development and Benchmarking
text:
8.7 Model Benchmarking
The candidate models are compared using a consistent evaluation framework.
Where possible, rolling-origin time-series cross-validation is used so that models are evaluated using only information that would have been available at the time of each forecast.
Forecast accuracy measures considered include:

Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)
Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE), where appropriate

Forecast behaviour and interpretability are also considered alongside numerical accuracy.

title: 8  Model Development and Benchmarking
text:
8.8 CPU and GPU Modelling
Where sufficient historical information is available, CPU and GPU demand are modelled separately.
This is particularly important for GPU resources because growth in AI, machine learning and other accelerator-intensive research may result in a different demand trajectory from traditional CPU computing.
If the historical GPU series is insufficient for reliable standalone forecasting, alternative scenario-based assumptions are considered rather than fitting an unnecessarily complex statistical model.

title: 8  Model Development and Benchmarking
text:
8.9 Modelling Limitations
The modelling approach is affected by several limitations:

a relatively short annual time series
changes in HPC systems and accounting methods
incomplete historical requested-demand information
supply constraints affecting observed allocations
limited historical GPU observations
changes in research classifications
some values being derived or estimated rather than directly reported

These limitations are considered when interpreting model performance and selecting the final forecasting approach.

title: 8  Model Development and Benchmarking
text:
8.10 Output
The output of this step is a set of candidate forecasting models and benchmark results.
These models are evaluated in the next step before the final forecasting approach is selected for scenario analysis to 2030.

title: 9  Model Evaluation
text:
9.1 Purpose
The purpose of this step is to evaluate the forecasting models developed in the previous step and assess how well they represent historical HPC demand.
Model evaluation considers forecast accuracy, residual behaviour, forecast behaviour and interpretability. The aim is not only to identify models with low forecast errors, but also to ensure that the resulting forecasts are reasonable for the available data and the purpose of the project.

title: 9  Model Evaluation
text:
9.2 Evaluation Approach
The candidate models are evaluated using a consistent framework.
Where possible, time-series cross-validation is used to assess how the models would have performed when forecasting observations that were not used during model estimation.
This is particularly important because evaluating models only on their in-sample fit may give an overly optimistic view of forecasting performance.

title: 9  Model Evaluation
text:
9.3 Time-Series Cross-Validation
Rolling-origin time-series cross-validation is used where the available historical data allow it.
At each evaluation point, the model is estimated using observations available up to that point and then used to forecast future observations.
The forecasting origin is progressively moved forward through the historical period.
This approach maintains the chronological order of the data and avoids using future information to predict the past.

title: 9  Model Evaluation
text:
9.4 Forecast Accuracy
Forecast accuracy is assessed using measures such as:

9.4.1 Mean Absolute Error
\[
MAE =
\frac{1}{n}
\sum_{t=1}^{n}
|y_t-\hat{y}_t|
\]
MAE measures the average absolute difference between observed and forecast values.


9.4.2 Root Mean Squared Error
\[
RMSE =
\sqrt{
\frac{1}{n}
\sum_{t=1}^{n}
(y_t-\hat{y}_t)^2
}
\]
RMSE gives greater weight to larger forecast errors.


9.4.3 Mean Absolute Percentage Error
\[
MAPE =
\frac{100}{n}
\sum_{t=1}^{n}
\left|
\frac{y_t-\hat{y}_t}{y_t}
\right|
\]
MAPE may be used as a supplementary measure where the observed values make percentage errors meaningful.
No single accuracy measure is used in isolation when comparing the models.

title: 9  Model Evaluation
text:
9.5 Residual Diagnostics
Residuals are examined to determine whether important patterns remain unexplained by the model.
The evaluation considers:

residuals over time
residual autocorrelation
unusually large residuals
systematic over- or under-forecasting
residual distribution

A well-performing forecasting model should not leave strong systematic patterns in its residuals.

title: 9  Model Evaluation
text:
9.6 Forecast Behaviour
The resulting forecasts are also examined visually.
This is important because a model can achieve relatively good historical accuracy while producing unrealistic long-term forecasts.
The evaluation therefore considers whether:

the direction of the forecast is reasonable
long-term growth is plausible
forecasts become unstable
prediction intervals appropriately reflect uncertainty
forecasts respond reasonably to the historical data

title: 9  Model Evaluation
text:
9.7 Structural Model Evaluation
For models containing structural demand drivers, evaluation also considers whether the estimated relationships are interpretable and consistent with the expected relationship between the variables and HPC demand.
Particular attention is given to:

coefficient direction
sensitivity to individual observations
model complexity
stability of estimated relationships
contribution of the selected drivers

Given the limited number of annual observations, model complexity is considered carefully.

title: 9  Model Evaluation
text:
9.8 Comparison with Benchmark Models
The structural models are compared with the simpler benchmark models developed in Step 7.
A more complex model is not automatically preferred simply because it contains additional explanatory variables.
The additional complexity should provide useful forecasting performance or interpretation relative to simpler alternatives.

title: 9  Model Evaluation
text:
9.9 CPU and GPU Evaluation
Where CPU and GPU demand are modelled separately, their models are evaluated independently.
This allows the evaluation approach to reflect differences in historical data availability and demand patterns between the two resource types.

title: 9  Model Evaluation
text:
9.10 Evaluation Limitations
Model evaluation is constrained by the relatively short historical dataset.
As a result:

the number of cross-validation periods may be limited
accuracy measures may be sensitive to individual years
structural changes may affect historical model performance
GPU evaluation may be based on fewer observations than CPU evaluation

These limitations are considered when interpreting differences in model performance.

title: 9  Model Evaluation
text:
9.11 Output
The output of this step is a comparison of candidate models based on forecast accuracy, residual diagnostics, forecast behaviour and interpretability.
The evaluation results are then used to support model selection in the next step.

title: 10  Model Selection
text:
10.1 Purpose
The purpose of this step is to select the modelling approach that will be used to forecast Australian research HPC demand to 2030.
The selection is based on the evaluation results from the previous step. Forecast accuracy is considered alongside model stability, interpretability, forecast behaviour and suitability for scenario analysis.

title: 10  Model Selection
text:
10.2 Selection Criteria
Candidate models are compared using several criteria:

out-of-sample forecast accuracy
residual diagnostics
stability of the model
plausibility of the resulting forecasts
interpretability
suitability for the available historical data
ability to support forecasting to 2030
suitability for scenario analysis

No model is selected based on a single accuracy measure.

title: 10  Model Selection
text:
10.3 Benchmark and Structural Models
The performance of the structural demand models is compared with the simpler benchmark models.
Benchmark models provide a useful reference for determining whether additional structural variables improve the forecasting approach.
Where a more complex model does not provide a meaningful improvement over a simpler model, the simpler model may be preferred.

title: 10  Model Selection
text:
10.4 Structural Driver Selection
For structural models, the final set of explanatory variables is selected based on both statistical performance and their relationship with HPC demand.
The selected variables should:

have a clear relationship with HPC demand
have sufficient historical coverage
be reasonably consistent over time
avoid unnecessary model complexity
support assumptions or projections to 2030
provide a useful interpretation for policy analysis

Given the limited number of annual observations, the final model is kept parsimonious.

title: 10  Model Selection
text:
10.5 CPU and GPU Modelling Approach
CPU and GPU resources are considered separately when selecting the final forecasting approach.
Different models may be selected for CPU and GPU demand if the historical data and demand patterns support different approaches.
Where the GPU time series is too limited for reliable statistical forecasting, a scenario-based approach may be used instead.

title: 10  Model Selection
text:
10.6 Expert Review
The modelling results and assumptions may also be reviewed with relevant HPC experts.
Expert feedback is used to assess whether the model assumptions, historical interpretation and resulting forecasts are reasonable in the context of Australian national research computing.
Any changes resulting from expert feedback are documented.

title: 10  Model Selection
text:
10.7 Final Model Selection
The final model or combination of models is selected after considering the quantitative evaluation results and the broader analytical requirements of the project.
The selected approach should provide a reasonable balance between forecasting performance, interpretability and robustness given the limitations of the historical data.
The rationale for the final selection will be documented together with the model specification and key assumptions.

title: 10  Model Selection
text:
10.8 Output
The output of this step is the selected forecasting approach for projecting Australian research HPC demand to 2030.
The selected model is then used as the basis for scenario forecasting and capacity-gap analysis in the final step.

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.1 Purpose
The purpose of this step is to use the selected modelling approach to forecast Australian research HPC demand to 2030 under different scenarios.
The scenarios are designed to represent different possible developments in Australian research activity and compute intensity rather than producing a single estimate of future demand.
The resulting demand forecasts are then compared with available or projected national HPC capacity to identify potential capacity gaps.
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.2 Forecast Horizon
The selected modelling approach is used to produce forecasts to 2030.
Forecast uncertainty is reported where appropriate to reflect the uncertainty associated with both the historical data and future assumptions.
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.3 Scenario Framework
Three main scenarios are considered:

Status quo
Restored national R&D intensity
AI acceleration

Each scenario uses the same overall modelling framework but applies different assumptions about the future development of relevant demand drivers.
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.4 Status Quo Scenario
The status quo scenario represents a continuation of current research and HPC demand conditions.
Future values of the structural drivers are based on recent trends or other reasonable baseline assumptions.
This scenario provides a baseline against which the alternative scenarios can be compared.
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.5 Restored National R&D Intensity Scenario
This scenario considers higher research activity associated with an increase in Australia’s research and development intensity.
Changes in relevant drivers, such as research funding and research activity, are translated into future HPC demand using the selected modelling approach.
The assumptions used for this scenario are documented explicitly.
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.6 AI Acceleration Scenario
The AI acceleration scenario considers stronger growth in compute-intensive research associated with increasing use of artificial intelligence, machine learning and accelerated computing.
Particular attention is given to GPU demand because these workloads may have different resource requirements from traditional CPU-based research computing.
The scenario assumptions are based on available evidence and are documented separately from the historical observations.
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.7 CPU and GPU Forecasts
Where supported by the available data, CPU and GPU demand are forecast separately.
This avoids assuming that CPU core-hours and GPU hours are directly interchangeable and allows differences in their future growth to be examined.
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.8 Capacity Comparison
Forecast demand is compared with available or projected national HPC capacity where suitable capacity information is available.
Demand and capacity are only compared where their units and definitions are sufficiently consistent.
The general capacity-gap calculation is:
\[
\text{Capacity Gap}_t =
\text{Forecast Demand}_t -
\text{Available Capacity}_t
\]
A positive value indicates forecast demand above the capacity represented in the comparison.
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.9 Facility-Equivalent Capacity
Where sufficient information is available, the estimated capacity gap may also be expressed in facility-equivalent terms.
This provides a more interpretable indication of the scale of additional computing infrastructure that may be required.
Any facility-equivalent calculation depends on assumptions about system capacity, resource type and utilisation. These assumptions are therefore reported explicitly.
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.10 Scenario Comparison
The three scenarios are compared to examine how different assumptions affect projected HPC demand to 2030.
The comparison focuses on:

total forecast demand
CPU demand
GPU demand
growth relative to the historical period
estimated capacity gaps
differences between scenarios
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.11 Uncertainty and Sensitivity
Scenario forecasts are not treated as precise predictions of future HPC demand.
Results depend on the selected model, historical data, conversion assumptions and future values assumed for the structural drivers.
Sensitivity analysis is used where appropriate to examine how changes in key assumptions affect the forecast results.
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.12 Policy Interpretation
The scenario results are interpreted in the context of Australia’s future national research computing requirements.
The analysis focuses on the potential scale and composition of future demand and the implications of different research and technology trajectories for national HPC infrastructure.
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis

title: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
text:
11.13 Output
The output of this step is a set of scenario forecasts to 2030 together with estimates of potential capacity gaps.
These results provide the main quantitative evidence used in the final technical report, policy summary and project presentation.
crumbs: 11  Scenario Forecasting and Capacity-Gap Analysis
